254.text:
Questions about health, politics and technology are answered in seconds on online forums, and many people think that online forums spread misinformation. I agree to some extent, since posts are unchecked, although many forums also share expert help.

To begin with, online forums can spread misinformation because posts are unchecked. Anyone can post opinions as facts, and popular replies are not necessarily accurate. A user who asks about a medical symptom, for example, may receive a dozen confident answers from strangers with no training, and some of the advice may be dangerous. People often trust a reply simply because many others agree, and false claims that are repeated can start to look true. Anonymous accounts feel no responsibility for what they write, and some deliberately spread rumours or promote products. Because discussions move quickly, corrections are often buried and the original mistake spreads.

However, forums also have positive aspects. Moderators, expert members and links to sources correct many errors, and communities for professionals, such as programmers or doctors, often provide high-quality advice. A beginner who posts a computer problem, for example, can receive a precise solution from an expert within minutes. Forums are also a place where people can compare experiences, which is valuable when official information is limited. Users must verify claims. They should check whether a reply cites reliable sources, compare several opinions and consult professionals before acting on advice about health or money. Forum owners can improve quality through clear rules, active moderation and tools that highlight verified experts.

In conclusion, I agree to some extent that online forums spread misinformation, but careful use and good moderation can reduce the risk.

263.text:
In a village or a small town, the weekly newspaper, the local radio station and the community website often provide the only news about what happens nearby, and this essay will discuss the role of local media in small communities, focusing on information and community identity.

To begin with, local media informs small communities about issues that national outlets ignore. A local paper or station reports council decisions, school events and local business, and holds officials to account. A resident who reads that the council plans to close a library, for example, can attend the meeting and protest before the decision is final. National channels rarely cover road repairs, planning applications or a missing pet, yet these affect everyday life. Local reporters know the area and can question mayors and officials, which makes corruption and waste harder to hide. Advertising in local media also helps small shops and farms to reach customers close by.

Furthermore, local media strengthens community identity. It celebrates local sports teams, festivals and achievements, gives space to residents' opinions and helps newcomers to feel at home. A radio programme in which elderly villagers tell stories about the past, for example, preserves memories and dialects that would otherwise be lost. In emergencies such as floods or snow, local stations provide immediate and relevant advice. However, falling advertising revenue and competition from online platforms make it hard for many small outlets to survive. Support from councils, donations from readers and partnerships with schools can keep them alive. When local media thrives, communities remain informed and connected.

In conclusion, local media plays an essential role in small communities by providing relevant news, holding authorities to account and strengthening a shared identity.

Củng cố bản sắc: đội thể thao, lễ hội, ý kiến cư dân, người mới; ví dụ chương trình radio người già kể chuyện bảo tồn ký ức, phương ngữ; lũ, tuyết cảnh báo kịp thời; doanh thu quảng cáo giảm, cạnh tranh trực tuyến; hội đồng hỗ trợ, độc giả quyên góp, hợp tác trường.
Vai trò thiết yếu.

274.text:
Magazines, television and social media fill daily life with pictures of famous people in expensive clothes, cars and houses, and many people think that celebrity culture encourages materialism. I agree with this view, since it presents luxury as the measure of success, although some celebrities live modestly.

To begin with, celebrity culture encourages materialism by presenting luxury as the measure of success. Constant images of designer clothes, cars and mansions make ordinary people feel that happiness depends on possessions. A young fan who sees her favourite singer buy a new handbag every week, for example, may start to believe that she needs the same brand in order to fit in. Programmes that show the homes and holidays of the rich make wealth appear normal and desirable, and advertisers use stars to sell products to millions of followers. Surveys suggest that young people who follow celebrity news closely place more importance on money and appearance and are more likely to run into debt.

However, not all celebrities encourage materialism. Some live modestly, give much of their income to charity or campaign for causes such as the environment and education, which shows that fame can serve other values. A footballer who funds a hospital instead of buying a fifth car, for example, sets a very different example. The influence also depends on the viewer, since families and schools can teach that character, effort and kindness matter more than possessions. Young people need alternative role models. Media can help by giving more attention to scientists, teachers, doctors and community leaders, whose achievements are based on knowledge and service and not on display.

In conclusion, I agree that celebrity culture encourages materialism, but its effect can be reduced by promoting different role models and values.

plan.think: Mở bài nêu hình ảnh người nổi tiếng xa hoa; agree.

Trình bày xa xỉ là thước đo thành công: hình ảnh quần áo, xe, biệt thự khiến người thường nghĩ hạnh phúc là tài sản; ví dụ fan trẻ thấy ca sĩ yêu thích mua túi mới mỗi tuần nghĩ cần cùng nhãn để hoà nhập; chương trình về nhà, kỳ nghỉ của người giàu làm giàu có hấp dẫn; nhà quảng cáo dùng ngôi sao; khảo sát: coi trọng tiền, ngoại hình, nợ.

Không phải tất cả: sống giản dị, quyên thu nhập, vận động môi trường, giáo dục; ví dụ cầu thủ tài trợ bệnh viện thay vì mua xe thứ năm; tuỳ người xem, gia đình, trường dạy nhân cách; hình mẫu thay thế: khoa học gia, giáo viên, bác sĩ.
Agree; giảm bằng hình mẫu khác.

284.text:
Advertisements show flawless models, spotless kitchens and products that promise happiness, and many feel that advertising creates unrealistic expectations. I agree with this view, since it presents edited images and exaggerated promises, although some adverts are honest.

To begin with, advertising creates unrealistic expectations of appearance and lifestyle. Edited models, perfect homes and promises of instant results make ordinary bodies and lives look inadequate. A woman who sees a skin cream advertised by a model with no visible pores, for example, may believe that the product will give her the same appearance, although the picture was altered by software and the model wears heavy make-up. Slimming products promise rapid weight loss without effort, and car adverts present empty roads and happy families, which do not match real traffic and daily stress. People who compare themselves with these images feel dissatisfied with their looks, homes and incomes, and they may buy more products in an attempt to close the gap.

Furthermore, unrealistic expectations can damage wellbeing, especially among teenagers who are still forming their self-image. Research links exposure to idealised bodies with low self-esteem and eating disorders. However, not all advertising is dishonest, and some campaigns now show diverse body types and real people. Honest labelling and diverse images reduce the harm. Laws can require clear notices when photographs have been retouched and ban claims that cannot be proved, while schools should teach students how images are produced. Consumers also have a role in treating advertisements with healthy scepticism.

In conclusion, I agree that advertising creates unrealistic expectations, but regulation and media education can limit its effects.

plan.think: Mở bài nêu người mẫu hoàn hảo, bếp sạch tinh tươm; agree.

Kỳ vọng phi thực tế về ngoại hình, lối sống: người mẫu chỉnh sửa, nhà hoàn hảo, kết quả tức thì; ví dụ phụ nữ thấy kem da quảng cáo bởi người mẫu không lỗ chân lông tin sản phẩm cho giống dù ảnh chỉnh, trang điểm đậm; giảm cân nhanh không cố gắng; xe đường vắng, gia đình vui; so sánh không hài lòng, mua thêm.

Hại sức khoẻ tinh thần nhất là thiếu niên: tự trọng thấp, rối loạn ăn uống; nhưng không phải quảng cáo nào cũng giả, nhiều chiến dịch cho thấy thân hình đa dạng; luật nhãn ảnh chỉnh, cấm tuyên bố không chứng minh; trường dạy cách ảnh tạo ra; người tiêu dùng hoài nghi lành mạnh.
Agree; quy định và giáo dục hạn chế.

302.text:
Famous actors, athletes and singers occupy magazines and screens in many nations, and this essay will discuss the benefits for a country that focuses on celebrity culture, using examples such as South Korea and the United States.

To begin with, a country with a strong celebrity culture gains tourism, cultural influence and fundraising power. Famous actors, athletes and musicians attract visitors and promote the nation abroad. South Korea, for example, has used its pop groups and television dramas to create worldwide interest in its language, food and fashion, and millions of tourists visit locations from their favourite programmes. Such soft power helps exports of cosmetics, electronics and cars, and it improves the country's image. Celebrity athletes can also inspire national pride during international competitions and encourage young people to take up sport.

Furthermore, celebrity culture supports a large entertainment industry and charitable giving. Film studios, record companies, fashion houses and media outlets create jobs for performers, technicians and designers, and their products earn export income. When stars campaign for charities, they can raise large sums quickly, as with the concerts and appeals held after natural disasters. Famous people also draw attention to causes such as the environment, health and education. The disadvantages include materialism, pressure on privacy and unrealistic images, but good regulation and attention to role models can reduce them. A country that manages celebrity culture well gains economic benefits and international prestige, while giving its young people examples of talent and hard work.

In conclusion, a country that focuses on celebrity culture benefits through tourism, cultural influence, jobs and fundraising, although the downsides must be managed.

326.text:
Videos of morning routines, extreme diets and expensive holidays attract millions of viewers, and many feel that online influencers promote unhealthy lifestyles. I agree to a large extent, since they are paid per click and rarely have medical training, although some influencers offer helpful ideas.

To begin with, some influencers promote unhealthy lifestyles by recommending extreme diets, supplements and constant spending. They are paid per click and rarely have medical training, so followers copy risky habits. A fitness influencer who claims that she lost ten kilos in two weeks by drinking only juice, for example, may persuade young viewers to starve themselves, and some of the supplements that she promotes have never been tested. Others encourage heavy drinking, unhealthy snacks or gambling, because sponsors pay for these messages. Pictures of perfect bodies and luxurious lives create pressure to look and spend in the same way, which can lead to eating disorders and debt.

However, not all influencers harm their followers. Others share fitness and cooking ideas that help, such as simple home exercises, balanced recipes and advice about sleep or mental health. A chef who shows how to prepare cheap, healthy meals, for example, can improve the diet of thousands of families. Many influencers also raise awareness of illnesses and encourage medical check-ups. Disclosure rules and critical viewers limit the harm. Laws should require influencers to state when they are paid and to avoid health claims that cannot be proved, platforms can remove dangerous content, and parents and schools should teach young people to question what they see and to seek advice from qualified professionals.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that online influencers promote unhealthy lifestyles, but regulation and media literacy can reduce the risks.

336.text:
Some users film strangers in distress, post children in humiliating situations or invent emotional stories in order to get attention, and many people think that exploitative behaviour on social media is harmful. I agree with this view, since it turns the suffering or trust of others into profit.

To begin with, exploitative behaviour on social media harms victims by turning their suffering or trust into profit. Some users film children or accidents for views, scammers use fake charities, and platforms reward shocking content. A parent who films a small child crying in order to produce a funny video, for example, may earn money, but the child is deprived of privacy and may be embarrassed for years when classmates find the clip. People who record an accident instead of helping gain attention at the expense of the victims and their families. Scam accounts that appeal for money for sick children cause donors to lose money and harm genuine charities. Vulnerable people, including the elderly and the lonely, are often targeted by fraudsters who pretend to be friends or partners.

Furthermore, such behaviour affects society by making cruelty and deception normal. Users learn that shocking or dishonest content earns rewards, which encourages more of it. However, not all attention-seeking is exploitative, and many creators earn a living honestly. Rules, reporting tools and public pressure are needed to limit the harm. Governments should protect children by regulating the use of minors in online content, platforms should remove scams and offer easy reporting systems, and users should refuse to share or reward exploitative posts. Education can also help people to recognise warning signs of fraud.

In conclusion, I agree that exploitative behaviour on social media is harmful, and it requires action by platforms, governments and users.

348.text:
Fewer people buy printed newspapers each year, and the question is to what extent traditional newspapers will disappear. I agree to a limited extent, since print newspapers will shrink and may largely disappear, but quality journalism will continue online.

To begin with, print newspapers are in long-term decline. Readers and advertisers have moved to digital platforms, making printing expensive. A local newspaper that once sold twenty thousand copies a day, for example, may now sell only a few thousand, and it cannot cover the cost of paper, ink and delivery. Young people get news from their phones and rarely buy a paper, and classified advertisements, which used to produce large profits, have moved to websites. Many titles have closed or merged, and some have stopped printing on weekdays. If this trend continues, print editions may become rare luxury items.

However, journalism itself will not disappear, and a number of newspapers are adapting successfully. Many titles keep subscribers and move to paid websites and apps, which give them a direct relationship with readers and allow them to produce investigative reporting. Some readers also value the paper format for long articles, for the feel of a weekend edition and for relaxing away from screens. A newspaper that publishes a weekly printed magazine with in-depth essays, for example, can still attract loyal customers. The medium will therefore change while news survives. Society needs trained reporters to check facts and to question those in power, and readers who recognise this value are willing to pay for it.

In conclusion, traditional printed newspapers will probably shrink greatly, but journalism will continue in digital form, so I agree only to a limited extent that newspapers will disappear.

354.text:
Television, streaming services and social networks offer unlimited content, and opinions differ on whether individuals should be responsible for their media consumption or whether society and government should regulate content. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of individual responsibility argue that adults can choose what to watch and learn to judge sources. A person who dislikes violent films can simply avoid them, and viewers can compare several news outlets to find reliable information. Parents can set rules at home, use filters and talk to children about what they see, and schools can teach media literacy. Freedom of choice is also a basic principle, and regulation by officials risks restricting opinions and art that they dislike. People who learn to question what they read become more independent and less likely to be manipulated.

On the other hand, supporters of regulation point out that children and vulnerable people need protection from harmful content, which only rules and platform duties can provide. Young children cannot judge a violent or sexual video, and adults may be misled by deliberate disinformation. A child who stumbles upon extreme material through an automatic recommendation, for example, has not made a choice at all. Media companies profit from attention, and without limits they may promote sensational content. Governments can require age checks, remove illegal material, demand transparency about algorithms and punish serious abuse. Media consumption needs both responsible users and sensible rules.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that responsibility should be shared: individuals and families should make informed choices, while society regulates clearly harmful material and protects children.

363.text:
Posters on the sides of buses and in metro carriages are seen by millions of passengers, and some people say that commercial advertising on public transport should be banned. I disagree, since advertising raises money to keep fares low, although content rules are needed.

To begin with, advertising on public transport raises money to keep fares low. Operators earn substantial income from adverts, which helps to pay for services. A city whose buses carry posters, for example, may collect millions each year, which can be used to maintain vehicles, lower ticket prices or run extra services at night. If advertising were banned, the revenue would have to come from higher fares or from taxpayers, which means that poorer passengers would pay more or that other public services would be cut. Adverts on trains and stations also help local businesses and event organisers to reach a large audience cheaply, and they can brighten otherwise dull spaces with colour and creativity.

However, passengers cannot avoid advertisements, and some images are offensive or unhealthy. Travellers who stand in a carriage are forced to look at posters for alcohol, junk food or unrealistic body images, and parents of young children may object. Rather than a total ban, strict content rules would be a better answer. Authorities can prohibit adverts that are sexist, violent or misleading, restrict promotion of tobacco, alcohol and unhealthy food on public property, and limit the number of adverts in each vehicle. Regulated advertising balances revenue and public interest, and it respects both passengers and operators.

In conclusion, I disagree that commercial advertising on public transport should be banned, but it should be regulated carefully.

Quảng cáo kiếm tiền giữ giá vé thấp: nhà vận hành thu nhập đáng kể; ví dụ thành phố buýt có áp phích thu hàng triệu mỗi năm bảo trì xe, giảm giá vé, thêm chuyến đêm; cấm thì tăng giá vé hoặc thuế, người nghèo trả nhiều hơn hoặc cắt dịch vụ; giúp doanh nghiệp địa phương, sự kiện, tô màu không gian.

Hành khách không tránh được, hình ảnh phản cảm hoặc không lành mạnh: đứng trong toa phải nhìn quảng cáo rượu, đồ ăn vặt, hình thể phi thực tế; phụ huynh phản đối; thay vì cấm hoàn toàn là quy tắc nội dung: cấm quảng cáo phân biệt giới, bạo lực, gây hiểu lầm; hạn chế thuốc lá, rượu, đồ ăn không lành mạnh; giới hạn số lượng; cân bằng doanh thu và lợi ích công.
Không cấm nhưng điều tiết cẩn thận.
